reading.body:
Oregon's 2026 legislative session produced no binding state law on artificial intelligence, only two AI bills that never passed and one executive order on procurement.

The pattern is a state regulating AI through the back door of procurement and data rather than through AI-specific statute. The two bills that name artificial intelligence, SB1546 on AI companions and HB4103, carry no status, which means they did not become law. What did pass is adjacent: SB1587 on data brokers, which governs the data that trains and feeds models, and SB5701 and HB5204 on state financial administration, the vehicles through which an executive branch buys technology. The September executive order on AI procurement safeguards fits that same channel, setting terms for what Oregon government itself will purchase rather than what private developers may build.

For AI specifically, this matters because procurement rules reach compute indirectly. A state that writes safeguards into its purchasing contracts shapes which vendors and systems can sell to it, and data broker law shapes the input side. Neither touches the binding constraints of siting, power, or interconnection, and nothing in this data addresses data centers, electricity, or grid capacity at all.

What the data does not tell the reader is large. It covers one state, one session, and fifteen bills, most of which are unrelated to AI. The two AI bills have no outcome recorded, so their failure is inferred from the absence of a status rather than stated. The executive order appears only as a headline with no text, scope, or effective date. Nothing here establishes how any of this is enforced, or whether it has changed what gets built in Oregon.
